utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Stefan Waespi, Matthias Neuner, and Daryl Mundis. We are assisted, as usual, by our case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, lead counsel; and Alexis Demirdjian, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Amir Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today, the 16th of March, 2005, the 198th day of the proceedings, I'd like to greet everyone present: The three members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, who are all present, and in particular Mr. Bourgon, who has returned from a trip abroad. I greet the two accused, as well as the witness, who is present, and everyone else in and around the courtroom. Today General Kubura's -- Mr. Kubura's Defence will be conducting its examination. Yesterday they said that they would need about 15 minutes. The Prosecution will then commence with its cross-examination, and we hope that we will have sufficient time to deal with the schedule for the coming days. I'll now give the floor to Mr. Kubura's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mujezinovic, we only have a few questions for you in relation to your testimony yesterday. I'd be grateful if you could answer these questions. In the course of your testimony, you mentioned the relationships between the Military Police Battalion and the 3rd Corps. You mentioned the relationships between the military police companies within the operations group. You said that the Military Police Battalion didn't have the right to issue orders to military police companies. For example, operations groups or to military police platoons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that military police companies, platoons, et cetera, were obliged to send to the Military Police Battalion daily or, rather, weekly reports? And you mentioned that there were numerous such reports.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But by order from the security sector, which resulted from a General Staff order, the military police units of a lower level had to compile weekly, that is to say, daily reports, and they had to indicate the number of measures taken as a result of the authority they had and they had to provide this information to their superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: This means that the reports were then forwarded to the security sector.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the Military Police Battalion was obliged to unify all the reports from the units of the military police of the 3rd Corps and forward them all to the chief of the security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: One more thing: When selecting personnel for the military police, for a battalion, for a company, for a platoon, it was the security sector that had the final word; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The superior organ for the military police was the security sector. For platoons and companies, they are the assistants of security and brigades. They were the people with most responsibility and it was their right and duty to participate in selecting personnel for military police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since I would like to show some documents to the witness, documents shown to the witness yesterday by General Hadzihasanovic's Defence, I'd be grateful if we could go into private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution. We are now in open session. You may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, just to clear the record in connection with the numbering. The document just discussed, tab 40, is DH1456, and I believe the document discussed before, tab 26, appears to be DH161, if I read that correctly. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My colleague is quite right. The first document we showed is DH161/8.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, we were just mentioning these criminal reports. Could you have a look at the series of documents, at document number 70 in this series of documents. It's Defence document DH1477. Have you had a look at the document?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Document 1477.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Criminal report against Ante Markanovic.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this case. Someone of this name falsely identified himself and then committed offences, and this report has recorded the case and it was forwarded to the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: He represented himself as a member of the 7th Muslim Brigade. He identified himself as such. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But he falsely identified himself. That was the crime he committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markanovic, Ante, against whom this report was filed, was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at page 2, the last paragraph in this document. Could you just mention the sentence. Ante Markanovic by the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that he was arrested by the military police of the 7th Muslim Brigade and was then handed over to the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: As the commander of the Military Police Battalion, you cooperated with the military police of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just as I did with other units of the military police and the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of cooperation did you have?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was professional and good.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I only have a few more questions for you about what you testified about yesterday, about the territorial jurisdiction of local units when carrying out military police duties. You said that units that have a -- that had a zone of responsibility in a given area had the duty and right to perform military police duties there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's answer was not audible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: If in that zone of responsibility there was activity carried out by local units and some other units were engaged with them, what sort of authority did the locally based unit have that had the zone of responsibility there?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The responsibility of a unit is defined by the order of a corps commander. He defines who shall be in charge of certain activities or of certain military duties that have to be carried out in that area. That person in that position of responsibility is responsible for carrying out activities in that area. All other duties that have to be performed by the military police, the engagement of military police in other areas has to be defined in an order, and it must be defined in terms of the relation of subordination or resubordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When combat is over, when the units who were in the zone of responsibility withdraw, the locally based unit continues to perform police duties in that zone.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the assessment of the assistant for security in the brigade or on the basis of an order from the commander for that unit, the military police stays on there for as long as it is necessary to establish full control over the unit until the unit withdraws from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: After the unit withdraws, they must continue to perform the duties that they performed before.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends. If that's the area of deployment of the unit, that's their duty. But if it's a civilian area that is then returned to the population and civilian authority is established there, then the civilian police had the authority and responsibility to take measures in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Afterwards, the civilian police has the duty to take measures for the protection of property and people who have remained in that area and they must take any other measures that they should take.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the civilian authorities are established, local authority, et cetera, then naturally the civilian police are part of that structure and that's their duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions. On page 8 in the transcript, I think there is no response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is an answer that hasn't been recorded. Could you put the question to him that was on page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to see what the question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The question was about territorially based units. They were responsible to carry out military police duties in their zone of responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now give the floor to the Prosecution for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness please be asked to speak up or could his second microphone be turned on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Could I suggest that before the Prosecution commences -- this is a witness to be cross-examined by -- by Mr. Waespi, and he has indicated to us that there are no less than ten new documents that he wishes to use. And in order to try and prevent lots of interruptions when the witness is testifying, could I suggest that if the witness is taken from the courtroom now, we address the issue of these ten documents immediately, and then the witness can be brought back once Your Honours' ruling is quite clear on the matter. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, will you please escort the witness for a few minutes outside and then Mr. Waespi is going to tell us about these ten new documents that I hear about now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it's because I'm not going to use, certainly not before the first break, these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If you're not going to use them. Mr. Dixon, the Prosecution tells us that they do not wish to use those documents before the first break. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Perhaps then, Your Honours, I'll suggest that when we come back after the first break we start, before the witness comes in, to discuss that issue, so that it's clear. Then when he comes if there are questions put about the new documents, there won't be lots of interruptions, because your ruling would have been made then, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Prosecution has the floor. You may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mujezinovic. I would just like to -- to clarify a few issues you discussed yesterday going over a few documents which you were shown by the Defence. Let me first ask you: You told us that you were the commander of the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps since 1st December 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And until when were you commander of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was commander of the battalion until the middle of 1997, about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us the names of the commanders of the military police companies, your direct subordinates, and also that service platoon during -- or for the time of, let's say, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the hierarchy, the most interesting in the chain of command was my deputy, Mario Opacak; the assistant for personnel was Branislav Tomas; the assistant for morale, Ismet Mudrov; assistant for logistics, Dzilo Sead; and the official for combat readiness, Durmo Edin; the commander of the military police platoon for investigations in 1993, that is, as soon as the battalion was formed, was Bakir Alispahic; and after that, Ruzmir Skopljak; the commander of the 1st Company was Nermin Dzambegovic; the commander of the 2nd Company, Adnan Becakcic; commander of the 3rd, Suad Fetic; commander of the traffic company, Mevludin Mustafic; and the commander of the logistics platoon, Nino Vareslija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you stressed yesterday but also this morning in response to a question by the Defence of Mr. Kubura the importance of the assistant commander for security for the deployment of the military police. Now, can you give me the name of the assistant commander for security of the 7th Muslim -- Mountain Muslim Brigade in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, but I think it was Nesib Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me briefly talk a little bit about your role as the battalion commander. Yesterday you mentioned in relation to Dusina, but we will go to Dusina a little bit later -- but you told us that the person in command of that military police investigations informed you that there was nothing in particular to be pointed out with regard to the prisoners of war. That's what -- what he told you. Now, let me ask you: Was it usual in the course of business that people who would interview suspects or witnesses would inform you about the gist of -- of their interviews? Was that a standard practice?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The chain of command says that the commander commands through subordinate commanders, and my contact along the chain began and ended with the commander of the subordinate unit. He's the one who carries out the deployment and engages his own subordinates on the basis of his judgement of their abilities. He is the person who after interviews were conducted filters the information through and provides the full information to me on the basis of which I inform the chief of the security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that you had the general knowledge about the investigations conducted within your battalion? Not the specific one, but the general knowledge, which enabled you to inform your superiors.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "General knowledge" would imply a complete report from my subordinate. If he assessed that he needed to inform me about certain elements, then you could say that. But in view of the fact that he is my subordinate and that I trust him fully, there's no reason to doubt that the information he gives me is complete information, and that is how I treat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. But my question was a different one: Did you, as the commander of the battalion, were aware of the investigations which were conducted by your battalion? Did you have a general knowledge about what types of investigations were -- were conducted?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, I did. However, if urgency called for certain operative work, investigations and so on, and I was physically not present, then that information would be presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the Dusina event, you were informed, I think very quickly, about what was contained in these interview statements; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends what you imply by "quickly." But that was the principle of work of the military police. In view of the fact that we had twofold orders, to collect information about the event, it was my duty to forward those reports to the judge and to the chief of the security sector. So probably that was one of the main reasons why this was done quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the quality of these -- the work of your interviewers. Were you generally satisfied about the work of the people who interviewed witnesses or -- or suspects? Could you rely on these witness interviews?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have too much chance of assessing whether it was of a good quality or not so good. But for me it was mostly important that on the basis of the security sector's assessment and my own insight up until then, the commander of the investigation platoon or the persons conducting the investigations have certain knowledge and qualifications. So I have no other resources. I consider them to be competent and capable of carrying out their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So can I just summarise that usually the witness statements being produced by your unit or by members within your unit were considered reliable?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me go to the broader subject of crime prevention. Yesterday you have given us the telling example of joint patrols between military, military police, and MUP patrols. In order to avoid situations, as you pointed out, that people would come and just say, "You know, I'm a civilian, so the military police doesn't have jurisdiction over me." Do you remember giving -- giving that example yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the reason for this smart move, I might add, is that there is no hole in crime prevention and indeed in -- in investigation, that no perpetrators can sort of walk away and say, "You know, that's not the jurisdiction of anybody." That's the purpose behind that -- that principle. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The aim of forming mixed patrols was prevention or, as you put it, full respect of the law and implementation of measures to detect and discover the perpetrators of the criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it's important, would you agree with me that, no crime sort of falls through the cracks on a given territory?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our duty, as well as of the civilian police, to do everything, to have all crimes investigated, and to take as many perpetrators to justice as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me briefly talk about the area of responsibility of -- of the 3rd Corps. You were shown one document yesterday. And perhaps we can briefly look into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's, Your Honours, Defence tab 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you can look through your documents, number 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the number is DH0746.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, sir, this is a order by the commander of the 3rd Corps dated 17 February 1993, and it's addressed to the Military Police Battalion. You talked about it yesterday. I am interested in just the last paragraph, number 6, where it says: "Submit the order to all brigade commands and the Municipal Defence Staff and publish it in modified form in all local information media in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps." Can you broadly tell the Trial Chamber the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, as outlined in -- in this order? Just very, very broadly.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you with precision. It depended on the situation and on the circumstances. The zone of responsibility was virtually where the 3rd Corps was deployed, and the units under the command of the 3rd Corps. What I do know is that there were certain changes when operative groups were formed as provisional entities, when the need was reduced or increased for the activity of the corps. So I can't tell you in general terms what the borders of the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But it was an area which was defined by borders. There were no islands inside the 3rd Corps area of responsibility which was controlled by somebody else. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no pockets until the beginning of the conflict with the HVO and the heightening of tensions in that area. Then pockets did appear because the HVO controlled certain territories which, according to the deployment, should have been covered by the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to the next document. That's at tab 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's DH161/13. And it's also, Mr. President, Prosecution Exhibit P158.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You have discussed that document yesterday, Mr. Mujezinovic, already. Here we see that the author, the command of the 3rd Corps, is "concerned about the protection of houses and personal property of Croat citizens." And I believe yesterday you also mentioned the attempts to protect a monastery, and the name was Kraljeva Sutjeska. There is also another document - and we don't need to go into that; that's tab 24 with your bundle - which also talks about the protection of -- of houses and property of Croat citizens. Now, having read all these -- these documents, is it correct to summarise that the 3rd Corps in its area of responsibility saw it as a duty to protect the property of the residents of all nationalities?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that not only extends to the property but also the physical well-being of these people and indeed their -- their lives.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the situation allowed, protection of property and lives applied to the areas where combat activities were going on and areas covered by 3rd Corps units. In other parts where there were no combat activities and where the civilian authorities are functioning, then it comes within the purview of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when we talk about the protection against whom, then the answer will be, "It doesn't really matter." It's whoever threatens the property or -- or the life of these residents. Is -- is that correct? Whoever is an alleged perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. But our primary goal was to protect them from irresponsible individuals and groups from the army but also from anyone else who may threaten the property and lives of the residents there. Not only of Serb and Croat ethnicity, but also of Bosniak ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And indeed, among the perpetrators - and you have listed them in that report that - I think it covered about the year. You were required to submit a report. And perhaps we can go later into that. That's tab 80. You listed the investigations, and I think there were 200 or more against ABiH members. There were about 200 against HVO members. There were about 200 against civilians. So it's -- it's fairly equal, the alleged perpetrators. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really remember the details, but as for the fact that they're roughly equal, it probably reflects the actual state of affairs on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps we can briefly go into tab 80. If you can have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, that's DH155/2, a document which has been used many times before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And on page 1, you see -- Mr. Mujezinovic, you see these numbers. I see your B/C/S copy is not very legible.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. The difference may be about 90. 206, 274, and 295. This probably shows that all categories, particularly in crisis situations, such as the shortage of basic means of livelihood, people tend to resort to such acts and that is why we have these figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it's correct to say that also foreigners, people outside countries from the former Yugoslavia, were among the people who threatened the local population in the relevant areas?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were there and if their behaviour was criminal in nature, then certainly they would have been a threat. If they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Because we heard testimony by a witness - in fact, he's a protected witness - who told us that certain Arabs had torched buildings in the area of -- of Guca Gora, and we have a corresponding exhibit in relation to that. Does that correspond with -- with your knowledge as well?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any particular knowledge about organised groups of Arabs in that area, but there were various groups of individuals who joined forces in order to gain unlawful profits or property. That is a fact. And in the description of our duties, this is stated and we tried to take measures and find evidence and submit criminal reports against such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me turn to the issue of civilian police and the interaction with the military police. We already discussed the -- the joint patrols. Can you confirm for us that the army could request the assistance of the civilian police for certain operations.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can confirm that the army, in relation to the military police -- I can confirm that the army requested assistance from the civilian police at the very beginning in 1992, before the formation of the corps. As an example, the Security Services Centre gave the military police company, or placed at its disposal, two police motorcycles to regulate military traffic. It wasn't a disgrace. It wasn't degrading. And the ABiH, depending on the situation, in particular military police, requested assistance from the Security Services Centre, given the personnel that they had and the equipment that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And for such operations, it -- it occurred that civilian police was subordinated, for instance, to the -- to a certain brigade. And I believe we have seen an example from the commander of the 306th Brigade, who, according to a document, commanded, in fact, the civilian police for a certain action.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my learned colleague yesterday requested that whenever I put a question to the witness, I should show the witness a certain document. My colleague has been asking a number of questions now by paraphrasing some documents and presenting the contents of the document to the witness. Since you accepted the suggestion made by my learned colleague yesterday, I believe that in the course of his cross-examination he should follow the same procedure; he should show the witness the document in question and only then put his question that concerns the document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You must have the document. All you have to do is show the witness the document immediately. You have it? Otherwise, ask the registrar to find the document and show it to the witness. Because Defence counsel believes that you might not correctly present a document and they would prefer the witness to see the document. You might not render the document accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I have no problem. There's a slight difference between cross-examination and -- and examination-in-chief, but I have no Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. problem. If the witness could be shown the Exhibit -- Prosecution Exhibit 204. And, Mr. President, we have a bundle of documents, as indicated by Mr. Dixon. And perhaps if tab 8 of my bundle could be shown to the witness. And perhaps you can take it apart, Mr. Usher, and only show the witness tab 8 of the bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, that would be simpler -- it's better not to destroy your binder. That's the document I had in mind, 204. We'll show it to the witness immediately. Mr. Registrar, you can take the English text back. I know it by heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujezinovic, this document, a -- an order by the commander of the 306th Brigade in paragraph 1 says that - and I quote - "All MUP and military police units of all brigades in the area of responsibility are resubordinated to the 306th Brigade." So that appears to confirm what I said before, that for certain actions, operations there was indeed a resubordination of -- of police units under the realm of the -- the army.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the protocol signed by the Security Services Centre and the 3rd Corps, it was possible to engage the civilian police, too, in certain situations. The commander of the 306th, in accordance with an order from the corps commander, availed himself of his right and units of the military police which were in the zone of responsibility of the brigade, together with the MUP, were placed under his command with that objective, to prevent looting, to protect property and persons in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. And we also had a witness who said that even police stations, civilian police stations were subordinated to the ABiH because the ABiH didn't have enough strength and also the soldiers were -- were exhausted. Have you heard of instances like that also?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any such situation, but given the needs, if certain territory was in the area of combat, if it was a matter of defending the territory, then the local commander, in my belief, had the right and duty to engage all the elements necessary for defence, including the MUP -- or rather, the police station in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The document can be returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I briefly want to discuss the -- the Rules of Service. You told us yesterday that you used them as a guideline. I believe you said they were -- they were issued on the 8th of September, 1992. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, and that's when they were issued. On the cover, on the blue cover, you could see the date, the 8th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, how important were these guidelines for you and the work of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guidelines were very important because they defined the relations in the chain of command. In terms of the Military Police Battalion, it defined its subordination and other elements in the organisation, in the structure, and also the norms according to which the military police had to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I have a copy available, but perhaps we don't need to show it to you, but you can -- you can request it if you don't know the answer for the next question, because in paragraphs 63 to 66 it always talks about an authorised official who is authorised to conduct certain powers, like detention and so on, in the absence of the military investigative judge. Can you tell us what and who this authorised official of the MP is?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the Exhibit P328 could be shown to the witness. Again, I would have a copy, but perhaps Your Honours prefer that we get the official copy from the registry.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An authorised official -- can I answer that question? An authorised official in the military police was someone to whom the military security service had issued a certain document -- or rather, the appropriate form of identification whereby he was authorised to be an official -- an authorised official. These people had been professionally trained. They were from military police platoons for investigations and they were in charge of conducting investigations and recording certain cases in order to file the relevant reports. Apart from the authorisation that they would receive, on the basis of the identity cards, they were guided by the Law on Criminal Procedure -- or rather, on the Law on District Military Courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for the answer, sir. That's all I wanted to know about the Rules of Service. Let me go back to a document we discussed before. That's tab 39 in -- in your bundle. We've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To save time, perhaps it would be good to ask the witness who, pursuant to Article 63, et cetera, would be appointed to this position. Was someone appointed? Was it just anyone? Who was this person referred to in item 63? Was it the witness himself or someone else?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much for this question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who would appoint this official? Was it you or somebody else? And was it always the same person who would be conducting these functions?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't always the same person. It concerned a number of individuals from the Military Police Battalion. And as I said, as a rule they were proposed by the battalion of the military police and they were authorised and received identity cards from the security sector confirming that they were authorised officials. These were primarily officers from the military police investigations sector, and they were involved in detective work, in operative work, and in finding perpetrators of crime. And there were certain persons within the chain of command who could take -- make use of this authorisation and seize objects, detain individuals for 72 hours. That was allowed according to the Law on Criminal Procedure at the time, et cetera. Basically these were authorised officials from the military police platoon for military police investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer, Mr. Mujezinovic. Let me return to document number 39. And I see you have found it already. Is it true that except for very few examples, you -- you never received an order to investigate crimes labeled as "war crimes" which involved members of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that on a number of occasions the witness explained the type of orders he had. He had to investigate all crimes. And I don't know what the basis of this question is from my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm just interested in -- in this aspect, which is a very important aspect of this trial, whether he was ever ordered by anybody to investigate any war crimes committed by members of the ABiH. I don't know what's wrong with this question. He can say "yes," he can say "no," he can explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you ever ordered by anybody to investigate into war crimes labeled as "war crimes" where the alleged perpetrators were soldiers or officers of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received orders to carry out investigations either by the security sector or by the judge, and it depended on the situation. When an order was issued to conduct an investigation, initially the type of crime wasn't defined or qualified. It was on the basis of the evidence that was gathered at the scene of the crime that a description of the crime was suggested and punishment for the perpetrators was suggested on that basis. As far as war crimes are concerned and other categories of crimes from that period, the sentences for such crimes were the same and would go up to the death penalty. So the description of the crime that we suggested to the court was in fact not binding on the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, let me turn, then, to this document which you discussed yesterday, tab 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, that's DH155, number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: On page 2 in the English version and also in your language, we have a heading "Four criminal disciplinary reports." And the second paragraph talks about several crimes which were discussed here. The first one was that a criminal report -- or two criminal reports were submitted against two individuals for the commission of a war crime against the civilian population under Article 142. And then the second -- the next paragraph talks about another war crime, pursuant to Article 119 of the SFRY Code, and it refers to "incitement to commit genocide and war crimes." Now, can you tell us, since you authored this report, what these two cases are about? Do you remember what it was about?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the report is from 1993, I really can't remember the details. About the criminal reports. This is a report for the specific period, for the month of August 1993. And the first part -- well, as far as the first part is concerned, I'm not sure. But the second case I believe concerns someone who served in the enemy army, and it was on that basis, service in the enemy army, a war crime against the civilian population was committed and there was incitement to committing genocide and war crimes and it was on that basis that this -- that a criminal report was filed against this individual. And we had good evidence for this in that certain documents had been compiled in the field. But as for the first case, I can't remember that because it's difficult to remember such reports, given that 11 or 12 years have passed since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is it possible that one of these war crimes concerned crimes occurring in the Balkovici camp? Do you remember that there was a perpetrator who was accused of crimes? He may have been the camp commander or warden. Do you remember that this might have been connected?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. You said it's a long time since 1993. I agree with you. But apart from these crimes labeled "war crimes," do you remember any other war crimes which were investigated by your battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me talk about the plan Golub - "pigeon," I understand from -- from yesterday - of January 1994. And this is tab 79.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I have got a draft translation of this plan, which perhaps could be distributed to the members in the courtroom. It even has holes, so you can put it into your binder.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which number?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I understand that you were among the three military commanders who were supposed to coordinate this -- this action. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was one of them, given the position I had. It was quite logical for me to be part of that team.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, how good was the intelligence you had on these 12 - I believe there are 12 people who were mentioned as alleged perpetrators - before you initiated that action which, I believe, started at 4.30 hours on 13 January 1994 in the morning? How much did you know about the -- these -- these 12 people?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operative activities to prepare this action had three aspects: Firstly, one had to go to the site and record all the situations in which these individuals perpetrated certain crimes, depending on the seriousness of the crime, and preparations had to be made to file criminal reports. At the same time, the military police security sector together with members of the Military Police Battalion and the assistant for security of the 314th gathered sufficient evidence -- sufficient information on their movement, on their joint activities, on their coordination in order to commit crimes and gathered other information that might be of use when arresting them. The operative work and the activities carried out to record everything and gather evidence to file reports against these 12 individuals lasted for a long time, six or seven months, I think. It was coordinated by the security sector and via the battalion and the assistant for security in the 314th. When complete information had been obtained and when the evidence was sufficiently good, in order to file criminal reports that would be accepted by the prosecutor, and after having consulted the prosecutor, these individuals were arrested. The information gathered was quite good because these individuals were army members, and on that basis the assistant for security in the units that they were parts of -- that they were part of could provide information on their movement, on where they were staying, et cetera. Our operative work involved supplementing this information. Then the security sector processed everything. And then we could proceed with their arrest, handing them over to the military prison, and to having the prosecutor state that they should be placed in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you had information, as we see in the report, the English version on -- on page 2, that - and I quote - "All persons encompassed by this plan are armed with pistols, automatic rifles, and hand grenades. They are very aggressive and inclined to offering active resistance using all available means." That's the information you had about -- among other information, about these alleged perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, among other things, that's the information that we had about them. There was only the minimum information stated with regard to the operation because we wanted to make sure that the level of security was sufficiently high for implementing this plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was the operation successful?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was very successful because very rapidly, in spite of the difficult circumstances at the time, in spite of the lack of equipment, the lack of vehicles and fuel and communications equipment, in spite of all of this, we successfully carried out the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me talk about a comment you made yesterday that -- what you called "a brief period in which" - and I quote you - "the practice that was followed was bad, so to speak, but the Chief of Staff tried to take over actions taken by the corps commander." In relation to your battalion, you said you don't remember the brief period, but can you place it somewhat into 1993, for instance? And please tell us more about what happened.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the date. I may be wrong. But this was indeed for 1993 but for a very short period, three or four weeks on the outside. What I said was that this was not the result of a wish for somebody to become more powerful in the hierarchy. It was the result of needs or the wish to relieve the commander of certain duties, because all the other units, and in addition to the Military Police Battalion there were others attached to the staffs, so all the units were linked directly to the Chief of Staff. I mentioned the Engineers Battalion, the Logistics Battalion, the Communications Battalion or Company, I'm not sure. The Anti-Electronic Struggle Unit. All these were directly linked to the Chief of Staff, with the exception of the Military Police Battalion. So in the aim of uniform activity in accordance with certain military rules, for a brief time the Military Battalion was within that group. There were no problems and very quickly on the basis of the proposal of the chief of the security sector and the decision of the commander, the old decision Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was restored, the only proper way of commanding the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But even during that brief period of time, the authority of the corps commander - commanded the 3rd Corps over his asset, the Military Police Battalion - wasn't put in question.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. The authority of the commander was never called in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's stay with the commander of the 3rd Corps for -- for a moment. I believe you said yesterday that you regarded the actions of the command of the 3rd Corps in relation to your battalion as -- as very professional. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And we have seen a number of documents shown to you by the Defence where the commander of the 3rd Corps directly ordered the military police for -- for specific action.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Depending on the need and the situation, the commander would give direct orders, and on the basis of his own judgement, and it was my duty to respect that judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Listening to you and also reading the document, it appears to me that the command of the 3rd Corps displayed a very good understanding into how the military police were operating. Do you share that?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an active participant in the events of the time. Not only do I share your opinion, but I'm absolutely certain that that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, perhaps that could be linked to the fact -- and I want to ask you whether you were aware of that -- that the command of the 3rd Corps at that time, General Hadzihasanovic, was himself the commander of a Military Police Battalion in the former JNA for four years. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. And it was an honour and pleasure for me to listen to advice and suggestions regarding the proper way to command the military police. But my impression is - that you referred to a moment ago - that not only did the military police have absolute support in their organisation and work, but I think that the other 3rd Corps units also enjoyed such support and that the commander was a commander in the real sense of the word, and he sought not to separate the military police from other segments, and it was my good fortune that I was able to get advice from a person who had such experience with respect to commanding of military police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, perhaps before the break we can touch upon a few brief issues. One relates to the Defence document in tab 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, that's DH156/1, tab 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is, again, an order by the commander of the 3rd Corps, dated 11th May 1993. And paragraph 1 correlates with something you testified yesterday about teams, inspection teams, which would be formed and touring the -- the area. I see that you are among the recipients of this order, the Military Police Battalion BVP. Now, do you remember, did that inspection occur? Did it happen, in relation to your own unit?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember, and the inspection did occur. I think that after this inspection we had some problems -- or rather, prior to the inspection, certain problems with logistics. That is, we needed to improve the organisation. And I remember in particular Rajko Velaga [phoen], I think he was a member of this team, he explained certain elements of logistics, because my assistant for logistics in those days had absolutely no -- no knowledge about the military hierarchy, the chain of command, and so on. And I remember the proposals that were made, and then there were an official proposal in the operations and teaching body that the situation as we had it was not satisfactory and that the proposal was made that an assistant for security be built into the structure so as to be able to cover this segment, and some other things that resulted from this inspection and direct assistance was given to the unit. All this is within the context of what I said a moment ago, that is, not only the Military Police Battalion but other units in the 3rd Corps enjoyed the same level and the same kind of treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, just before the break - we have about five minutes - let me turn to tab 21, again from your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Mr. President, this is DH160/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is a document dated 27th March 1993, and it comes from the assistant commander for security of the 3rd Corps. I'm interested in the second page, item 3, "Formation of special purpose MUP units."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I may be of assistance to my learned friend. In our language, the translation was "document 25" and I'm afraid the witness will not be able to find the document. Actually we are talking about tab 21. So as to avoid any confusion, I thought I'd say this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I appreciate your help. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Document 21, item -- item number 3, on the -- on the second page, "Formation of special purpose MUP units." And it says, 3 subparagraphs: "The 3rd Corps commander and the centre CSB Chief of Staff are to agree on the location for accommodation of the centre CSB special purpose units." It talks about replenishment in relation to the BH army, weapons, and equipment. Do you know something about this special purpose MUP units?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. And on the basis of this information and as a result of an agreement between the Security Services Centre and representatives of senior commanders of the 3rd Corps, lead to further activities to set up special purpose units in the CSB of Zenica. I know that in the area of Zenica specifically the MUP formed a detachment called "Manoeuvre," and that its involvement in combat operations depended on agreements between the corps commander and the chief of the Security Services Centre that the principle of replenishment was also agreed at the level of this commission so that there wouldn't be any undesirable situations. For example, somebody from the BH army because of more favourable conditions in this unit might leave his original unit with his weapons, and that is why these points were agreed on, that is, that the replenishment and supply of weapons should be carried out in coordination with the 3rd Corps command, which again implied that in the future their involvement would be decided between the corps command and the centre of the security services.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, why would the BH army -- some BH army members favour these special units? Did they have better weaponry, better conditions, better uniforms, paid better? What was favourable?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've listed most of it: A better uniform, better conditions, shorter working hours, better pay, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And would you consider these units to be elite units?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Objectively, it's difficult to say what an elite unit is. Apart from the human potential, for someone to be elite, he would have to have the necessary materiel and equipment. I can't say that they were an elite unit but that they were better equipped that many other BH army units. That I can claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And were they also better trained and in that sense better to be used for specific operations?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were better trained in the classical police sense, as these were mostly members of the active-duty policemen or reserve policemen, which meant that in the previous period they had undergone training lasting from six months to one year. So in the classical police sense, they were certainly better trained than members of the army. As for combat, I'm not quite sure because I don't know what tactical training they had to be better equipped for that type of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would they have been suitable to be used for the action Golub in January 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never really thought about that. These were members of the BH army. These were activities within the jurisdiction of the district military court. And these were jurisdictions belonging to the military police. The chief of the sector and I personally felt that we had qualified people and that we were capable of carrying out that plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Perhaps it's a good moment to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're going to have a break. And we will resume at about five to 11.00. And when we do, I shall give the floor to the Prosecution for them to tell us about the 10 documents, if they intend to use them later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I shall give the floor to the Prosecution to address the question of new documents. But I wish to point out that we have ruled on these matters on a number of occasions. The Prosecution, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, I have the bundle available, except for my friend Mr. Dixon was -- received a complimentary copy yesterday. I believe nobody has it. But I can start talking and briefly explaining what I intend. And perhaps if you want to see the documents, that's fine. But let me first point out: As you said, Mr. President, I might not use these documents. If the witness remembers the -- the incident, then that's fine. And if I think it's credible what he's saying then -- or -- it's not always credibility but also, you know, other issues, then I might not use it. So having said that, I intended to use five documents which are labeled "new." There is one exception or one document which is different because that one document we obtained only in -- on the 23rd October 2004, which was after the Prosecution closed its case. So I believe that for that document we -- we have different rules. So it could be used as evidence, understand, for its full purpose, not just credibility and memory refreshing, as far as I recall your ruling. So these are the -- the five documents. I can go through them one by one, if you wish me to do. But it might perhaps be easier to -- to do it when I intend to use it. But I'm in your hands, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours are absolutely correct. The rulings have been clear in the past. There is just a -- a new matter that has arisen in respect of -- of three of the documents. And perhaps my -- my learned friend can indicate whether or not those three documents are to be used. Because if they're not, then there's no need for me to address Your Honours further. And those are documents 16, 17, and 18. They are three statements taken by the 3rd Corps military police from witnesses, witnesses who have not appeared here before Your Honours. And in my submission, that is an entirely new matter, whether or not these statements can be used with this witness. If the witness who made the statement is not and has not been called by -- by the Prosecution, made available for us to cross-examine that witness. So perhaps my learned friend could indicate if those statements are going to be used. If they're not, then I'm not going to seek to address Your Honours any further. If they are, then I would wish to address Your Honours in order to clarify what is the status of those statements. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon, who is a specialist for new documents, tells us that he has noted that there's a new case now which was never raised until now, and that is document 16, 17, and 18 are statements of witnesses taken apparently by military police officers, and the problem, according to the Defence, is that it is difficult to show documents to somebody who did not take those statements himself and is not familiar with those statements. That is what the Defence is saying. So if you don't intend to use those documents, the matter is resolved. If you do intend to use them, please respond to the remarks made by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, I intend to use just one out of these three ones. That's number 17. Although --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which one? Seventeen. I see. Could you tell us what is this document? What is its date? Who is the author, et cetera. Because we shall have to deliberate on the matter. So give us some information, when you obtained that document, where does it come from, and all the other necessary information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That's a record of a witness or suspect interview done by the Military Police Battalion. The commander is testifying today. And it dates 7th March 1994. We have received these documents in a -- I understand a search operation, I believe, consensual. It's, I think, in the CSB archives, and we accepted it in March -- February and March of 2004. So that's clearly within your ruling; meaning, I can use it to refresh the memory of this gentleman or in relation to his credibility. And, Mr. President, I don't need -- I don't want to use it as such, as evidence, the interview. That's very important for you to realise that. We don't want to sneak in a witness statement. We're just going to the information which is provided in the statement. I will ask him. Because it's very specific. He talks about people coming from Turkey, being interviewed by members of the military police. And perhaps this gentleman, being the commander of the Military Police Battalion and having said this morning that he was generally appraised, as he should be as the commander, of what his people were doing, he might give you some knowledge about these interviews with these people who came to Bosnia as -- under disguise of humanitarian assistance. I think if the witness can say something about that, that would be for -- of your assistance. And just one correction: These documents don't come from the CSB archive but from the ABiH security archive. Yes, and perhaps a second point: I believe the Defence also showed the statement of Ramo Durmis to -- presented to one of the, I think, Prosecution witnesses, one of the judges -- Defence witnesses. So there is a precedent for using witness statements. And there shouldn't be any difference between -- in cross-examination, between using information stemming from a document or stemming from a witness statement. The underlying information, that's the important thing, and not the form. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand your position properly - I would like to summarise it - and that is that you would like to use this document simply to refresh the memory of the witness. But before refreshing his memory, you have to ask him questions without using the document. That's quite normal. And if his replies remain vague or evasive, then you can say, "Here I have a document which says," so and so, "what does it say to you?" Mr. Dixon, to refresh the Judges now, what can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours are entirely correct that my learned friend is entitled to use these documents to seek to refresh the memory of the witness. My only concern, as Your Honours pointed out, is that he should lay a proper foundation first, to ask whether or not he snows anything about these particular incidents. And only if the witness says, "Yes, but I can't remember," then may he take the next step of saying, "Well, would a document assist you?" Bearing in mind that this witness's name does not appear on this document at all, though my learned friend said very clearly yesterday when Mrs. Residovic tried to show a document to the witness that he hadn't signed that -- he objected to that, because there's no worth, he said. "It's not helpful," were his words "in trying to lead document that he had nothing to do with." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So that's the first point, Your Honours. But the second and the most important is that if my learned friend wishes to use this document to make assertions about the information contained in the witness statement, he's free to do that because he has a good-faith basis, as he said many times before, that's all he needs, a good-faith basis for doing that. But our objection is that this document cannot come into evidence unless the particular witness who made the statement is to be call by the Prosecution. They haven't done that up until now. He's free to make assertions based on the statement and to see what the witness says. But if the witness says that he disagrees with those assertions, then in our submission, that is the end of the matter. The statement itself cannot be introduced into evidence. The only way that can happen is if the witness comes or 92 bis is used or if there's 89(F) as well, but for that reason the witness has to be here to attest to the statement. Your Honours, I also do wish to draw your attention to a decision in the Milosevic case, which I cite in support of my submission, where there as well the Prosecution tried to introduce statements of other witnesses through a witness in court who hadn't signed that statement. So it was another witness in court. And he was shown a statement of a third or fourth witness. And there Judge Robinson ruled very clearly - and it was on the 28th of February, 2005, at page 36814 - that "These statements have not proceeded beyond the level of being mere assertions. At no time did the witness agree with any of the propositions advanced by the Prosecution in relation to the information in these documents, so they are not admitted." That was the ruling of -- of the Trial Chamber in respect of the witness statement, saying it cannot be admitted for the truth of its contents. The only way that can happen is if the witness himself is called. And I point this out because I accept what my learned colleagues said, that they're not trying to sneak something in. But if he is to make assertions about what is contained in the statement, then the statement itself cannot be introduced, unless, of course, the -- if the witness adopts the statement as true. That's different. But it cannot be introduced unless the Prosecution seek to call the -- the witness himself. Your Honour, finally, I did just want to point out that in respect of the document for Mr. Durmis, that was a new document that the Prosecution themselves sought to introduce. And we were then, once it was in evidence for a limited purpose, putting it to further witnesses that were called. That is also a different document in the sense that it was taken formally in court proceedings under oath; whereas, this statement is one taken not under oath, without caution. It's simply a statement taken by the military police as part of their investigations. So it's a very different situation. The one is a court record; this is in the form of a witness statement, and it cannot come into evidence, in our submission, unless the witness is actually called to testify and we are given the right to cross-examine the witness about what is in this statement. Your Honour, those are our submissions. We don't have any objection to the document being used in the way that has been described by my learned friend, to seek to refresh his memory. But it cannot be shown unless he actually needs it, if he actually does forget and say, "I want a document." And in addition to that, it can't be used as evidence. It can't be used to strengthen the Prosecution case in any way. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the Prosecution would like to respond, but in our decision dated the 29th of November, 2004 we dealt with this issue and we settled the matter. We said that the Prosecution can refresh a witness's memory, just as the Defence has said. It's not a new exhibit, a new piece of evidence. But if the Prosecution is requesting that this document be admitted into evidence, it can only be admitted in a limited sense and can only be used to establish the witness's credibility or to refresh a witness's memory. It's not a new exhibit. This document can only be used to refresh a witness's memory. This is what Mr. Dixon has said and he has supported his arguments with reference to the Milosevic case. Would the Prosecution like to respond before the Judges deliberate?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We agree with what you said and most of what my learned friend said, and I've said in my first submission, we don't want to use it as evidence -- submit it as evidence. It's only evidence what comes out of the mouth of this witness and not what -- what I'm saying or what's in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite right. You don't want to use it as evidence, but we shouldn't exclude the following hypothesis: When refreshing the witness's memory, you might say that -- or you might at the end say that you are requesting that this exhibit be admitted into evidence in conformity with your decision on refreshing a witness's memory. Is that what you are stating? Yes, very well. We will withdraw now and we will return in a few minutes. --- Break taken at 11.18 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to this procedural issue, the Trial Chamber notes that there is more or less agreement between the parties. In accordance with our decision, on page 12.526, the Prosecution may refresh a witness's memory by using a new document but provided that before refreshing the witness's memory the Prosecution establishes the grounds by putting a series of questions that will lead up to presenting the document shown to the witness to refresh the witness's memory, and it's sufficient at that point to show the witness the document, but it's necessary to establish the grounds. And it's only if the witness answers the question in relation, which doesn't seem to tally with the document, that you can refresh the witness's memory by using the document. But as we said in our decision on page 12.526, the document can only be admitted in a very limited sense. We'll now call the witness back into the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you just check to see that if we are unable to finish the examination of this witness today, we could continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing will now resume, and the Prosecution may continue with its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would first ask your leave, Mr. President, to ask him a few questions about Mr. Ramo Durmis. You remember that a subordinate of Mr. Durmis, Mr. Semir Saric came on Monday and testified and he was allowed to answer a few questions about Mr. Durmis. And he said that he was aware of an investigation which was connected by colleagues of -- of his; meaning, members of the military police, who investigated that matters. And that relates to an incident towards the end of 1992 in the clashes in the territory of Visoko, attempts to deblockade the city of Sarajevo. And just to correct the record, the transcript, the witness Mr. Saric, Semir Saric, he was a subordinate of today's witness, Mr. Mujezinovic, and of course not Mr. Ramo Durmis. So there are no new documents involved. I would just like to ask him a few questions, if he knows anything about this incident to which the witness on Monday alluded to on page 65, lines 10 to 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're saying that the subordinate of the witness, who is present, Mr. Semir Saric, mentioned the existence of an investigation into events that took place in the territory of Visoko and you want to know whether the witness here today is familiar with this. Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this witness has said that he had between 250 and 400 subordinates in the Military Police Battalion. The witness Semir Saric was here, and the Prosecutor asked Semir Saric everything that he could ask Semir Saric at the time. I'm sure of that. And I, in the course of the examination-in-chief, didn't mention any events in the area of Visoko, nor do I mention -- nor did I mention Ramo Durmis. I think that there's no legal basis -- or the testimony of a previous witness can't form a legal basis for putting such a question to this witness, and for this reason I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We had this debate about the ambit of Rule 90(H), I think it is, a couple of times, and that's why I ask leave, Mr. President, just to ask a few questions about Ramo Durmis. And you granted leave to my colleague Mr. Neuner on -- on Monday to ask a few questions about Mr. Durmis. Now, Mr. Durmis is quite a prominent figure, as -- as you know. And perhaps the commander of the military police whose subordinates, you know, were able, despite the fact that he was not involved - the witness on Monday - was still able to talk a little bit about Ramo Durmis. So perhaps this gentleman can -- can do the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll withdraw for a few minutes. --- Break taken at 11.26 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will now render a second decision today, with regard to whether the Prosecution may ask the witness a question. The Chamber believes that the name of this witness has already appeared in the course of the proceedings and that the document refers to this witness. And, in addition, a subordinate of this witness has already answered a question about Mr. Durmis, and it would be in the interest of justice to put a question to the witness. He will either answer the question or he won't answer the question. So please go ahead and put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I'm sure you remember the -- the person Semir Saric as one of your former subordinates?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, he told us on Monday that in relation to Ramo Durmis, "That he was often searched by our services." Now, can you tell us, if you know anything about this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that he was well known. I wouldn't say that he was a particularly well-known person to me. As far as I know, thanks to some postwar events - and that's what I know about - a criminal report was filed against Mr. Durmis, perhaps together with the Security Services Centre or perhaps they acted on their own. It had to do with the abuse or the seizure of motor vehicles. I'm not certain of the proceedings, the nature of the proceedings, or of the sentence at the court. After the war, I became familiar with Mr. Durmis -- or rather, I came to know him and he took advantage of the opportunity to say that he was the person concerned, that he was Ramo Durmis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us in -- in what setting you became familiar with Mr. Durmis after the war.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He lived in the same building that I lived in. He was a neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go back to 1992 Visoko. We heard from your subordinate that there were -- was some incident in December, I believe, 1992 around Visoko. Have you heard about that, that incident?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of such an incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We have an exhibit, but perhaps it's no need to show it to you, where Mr. Durmis reports about the operation of the 1st Company in the Visoko-Buci-Rakovci-Visegrad elevation sector. You don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why Ramo Durmis would report to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's not to you. It's just basically he was asked to make a report about these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Your Honours, just for the record, but we won't go into that, that would be P514.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But since you haven't heard anything about that event, Visoko, Ramo Durmis, we won't go into that.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
