utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's talking about Dusina, Mr. Mujezinovic. Now, I'm not entirely sure whether I understood your testimony yesterday. I believe you said that an on-site inspection was carried out in Dusina. And I quote you. You said: "A team was formed and sent," page 62 -- 76, of LiveNote of yesterday. What do you know about this team that was formed and sent, and do you know whether it appeared at Dusina, if that's what you mean? And Dusina, that's obviously 27th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that a team was sent to carry out an on-site investigation in Dusina. I said that after information from the civilian protection was obtained, this duty service sent a team to carry out an on-site investigation together with the investigative judge in the morgue of the cantonal hospital in Zenica, where the corpses had already been taken to from the Dusina area. The prosecutor -- or rather, the judge in charge of the investigation assessed that the members of the units that I commanded weren't sufficiently well equipped to carry out the investigation, and he ordered that a patrol from the Security Services Centre remain at the site and the patrol from the Military Police Battalion was returned by him back to the barracks, and it was their duty to provide statements of the individuals imprisoned who were taken from Dusina to the Centre for the Reception of POWs. According to the information I obtained from my subordinates, these statements were taken, and on the basis of this order they were forwarded to the judge in charge of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, I thought you cleared it up first by saying there was no on-site investigation carried out in Dusina but, rather, at the morgue and hospital, which is an information we heard from somebody else. But now later you say that the "Security Services Centre" or "a patrol from the Security Services Centre remain at the site." Can you tell us more about -- about that? What were these people doing at the site? And by "site" do you mean Dusina?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "site," I'm referring to the morgue of the cantonal hospital in Zenica. At the time, I don't know what its name was, but it was the hospital in Zenica. That team was a forensic team, and its objective was to determine the circumstances under which these people had died. This involves analysing the wounds, describing the corpses, performing the paraffin test on the individuals killed in order to determine whether they had used firearms, and it also involves carrying out all the other analyses ordered by the judge who is at the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thanks very much for this answer, which clears up the matter, because we had another witness, a prosecutor, Mr. Ragib Hadzic who looked into the matter in 1999 or 2000 and told us that no on-site investigation was carried out in Dusina. He also said, though, that he could not find any records of witness statements taken in the file he reviewed. Can you give us an explanation why the witness statements which you mentioned today and yesterday and, by the way, also your colleague on Monday, weren't part of that official file which Mr. Hadzic reviewed -- reviewed in 1999 or 2000?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the reasons for which the statements are not included in the official files that Mr. Hadzic reviewed, but I can claim with full responsibility that the statements of prisoners of war in the reception centre were forwarded to two addresses: They were forwarded to the judge in charge of the case in the military cantonal court, and to the chief of the security sector in the 3rd Corps. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the name of the judge in charge of the case in the military cantonal court, that's Mr. Mirsad Strika?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know what he did or was supposed to do with his file?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can assume what he should have done. I assume that on the basis of those statements he should assess whether it was necessary to take any other measures. And naturally it was necessary to bear in mind the investigation carried out in the morgue, and this should have allowed him to determine whether there were grounds to take further measures, whether there were grounds to order that certain individuals should be brought in, interrogated, whether evidence should be collected, et cetera. When he went to the site, Mr. Strika became the person who had the highest responsibility, and his orders, his instructions were the only valid guidelines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So what was the measures which he was supposed to take after having assessed the material, went to the site?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can assume what they were, because Mr. Strika was a judge from the regional military court. He was very experienced and probably sufficiently professional to take a decision on his own, but I assume that if there were grounds to continue with an investigation or if there were indications pointing to the fact that a crime had been committed, then he should have ordered steps to be taken in order to shed light on the crime. If he assessed that everything was the result of combat, he could quite simply complete the case, shelve the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Without going to the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I'll repeat what I said: Mr. Strika was sufficiently professional and sufficiently experienced, in terms of his works in the military courts, to know what he should have done, but I can't say what he did. I can only assume what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would you have gone to the crime scene yourself to see what was happening

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Believe me, I haven't given any thought to the matter. But bearing in mind the fact that according to information I had, immediately afterwards there was shelling in that area and even civilian areas were indiscriminately shelled, I'm not sure that I would have gone to the scene at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Among the people interviewed by your subordinates, was there Ivica Kegelj, one of the perhaps two survivors of that killing not through shelling but through a killing, a execution in Dusina? Did your people interview Ivica Kegelj?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the names of the prisoners interrogated by my men. Perhaps I had a look at the list at that time, but given the passage of time, I can't remember the names of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you think they should have interviewed one of the survivors of that incident, a person by the way who was asked to put the bodies of the killed, executed persons into his garage? Do you think that would have been a person who needed to be interviewed in an investigation into the killings of these people?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object to this question, too, because my learned colleague is now interpreting some facts that he had not previously asked the witness about, whether he was aware of a garage, of people in a garage, of people being killed, where the bodies were found in this vast area, in the course of combat. These -- such questions, if they had been previously put to the witness, could provide him with grounds for this question, but he's now asking the witness about bodies being placed in a garage. I see no grounds for putting this question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel objects because the Prosecution hasn't established the grounds to put this question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But the members of your military police who conducted this inquiry or investigation, they had access to all the people who were detained at the KP Dom, who were brought from Lasva Valley to -- from Lasva to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the people who were brought to the Reception Centre for Prisoners of War from Dusina were available to authorised officials from the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it would have been the task of an investigator - and I think you said there was someone in charge - to find the survivors of this incident; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If an investigation is launched into alleged incidents which occurred or may not have occurred, if somebody who looks into that, would he try to find eyewitnesses to a crime?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty judge is in charge of the investigation, who goes on site. The Military Police Battalion was ordered to take statements from persons who arrived at the Reception Centre for Prisoners of War. Apart from that order or instructions, no one, me, or my superior, the chief of the security sector, or the corps commander cannot influence the course of the investigation. We were ordered to take statements from people in the centre and thereby our duties end. Had the judge ordered us to carry out certain checks, to investigate in the ground, to look around for those you called "survivors," we would have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So on that evening or on that morning, who picked the names of the people your subordinates had to interview?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My subordinate commander of the platoon for investigations, Mr. Bakir Alispahic, had the lawful duty to assign the persons who would interview which of the war prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you are saying Mr. Alispahic, he assigned the members of the police battalion, the interviewers. But who is picking the people to be interviewed?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the person who would say, "Three prisoners of war," and their names and initials or whatever, and he would assign an authorised official from among his staff to do the interviews. So he selects both the authorised official and the prisoners who will be interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when you testified yesterday that the person in charge of the investigation had informed you about these interviews and you said they were done according to the rules and regulations, it was Mr. Bakir Alispahic who reported to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did your unit, Mr. Bakir Alispahic, apart from merely sending the statements to -- to the investigative judge -- did your services also make a report about the investigation?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not prepare special reports about the investigation because we were not authorised or competent to do so. We would just forward the statements, as I have said, but we did not prepare complete reports, nor were we expected to do so. But only about the part of the investigation relating to the examination and interviewing of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Isn't the military police, the investigators, required to draft reports about alleged criminal activities? Isn't that one of -- one of your jobs? And we have seen many of these criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're going back to the competencies and jurisdiction. I am saying the taking of statements requires instructions from the investigative judge. He is the person. As he is on site, he's in charge of the investigation and he determines whether there are any elements of criminal liability or any other kind of liability and gives instructions regarding some other measures. So we did file criminal reports. We did send reports about the investigations we conducted independently when there was no judge who was in charge. We proposed measures in accordance with our obligations, and when we coordinated efforts with the chief of security. But in this particular case, our task, following instructions from the investigative judge, was simply to take statements in order to collect as much information as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to finalise two small aspects to what you just said. You said you had coordinated efforts with the chief of security. In relation to Dusina, did you have any interaction with the security service or indeed anybody else from the 3rd Corps outside your battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first contact, with the chief of security, when we were given direct orders to take over the prisoners and escort them to the Reception Centre for Prisoners of War. The second contact was when the chief of security, after contacting the judge regarding statements to be taken, that is when we had a contact with him. And the third time was when the statements taken from the prisoners of war were forwarded to the chief of the military security sector for his information, because he, too, didn't have the competence to undertake any other measures, as the judge was in charge of the investigations on the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the first contact, when you were given direct orders to take the people from -- the prisoners from Lasva, do you remember when that was? Which time of the day it was?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date. It was the end of January 1993, late in the afternoon, but I know that the commander for military police investigations informed me in the evening that the -- he had carried out the orders I had passed on to him, that is, that he had escorted the prisoners to the reception centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you talk directly to the chief of security before you gave the assignment, you know, of your military police to go to -- to get the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I spoke to him, because I received the order directly from him for the Military Police Battalion to take over the prisoners. That was the first contact we had in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what exactly did he tell you? And incidentally, was that over the phone, or how did that conversation occur?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversation was over the phone, but I find it hard to recollect the details. He told me, to the extent one could speak on the phone, that in the Lasva region -- or rather, in Dusina there had been certain combat activities, that this was -- had resulted from earlier tensions, and that the unit in the area had captured a certain number of prisoners. And he ordered me to organise the escort of those prisoners from Dusina to the reception centre at the KP Dom. My concern was to select the people and the necessary means for transport. And I know that we engaged a large bus for the purpose, to be able to carry out our task properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about killings, casualties, civilians, military, ABiH, HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say anything about that. We didn't discuss it. But the next day in a conversation he mentioned that there had been casualties on both sides, that apparently there had been casualties whose method of death cannot have been established, that the civilian protection had already sanitised the battlefield, and that the number of killed people in Lasva had already been transported to the morgue in Zenica. About the same time, we received information from the duty service from the civilian protection, so that within a short span of time of some 10 to 20 minutes both these reports reached the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did he also tell you that one of the ABiH commanders, the company commanders, was killed?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that on our side, according to available information, there had been dead, but he didn't mention of what rank. He just said that there had been some dead. And later on I learnt that was the commander of one of the units, again from a report of the chief of the security sector that I learnt this subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And his name was Elvedin Camdzic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying that I learned subsequently that it was Mr. Camdzic, whom I didn't know personally, so I can't be more specific about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember that in relation to this gentleman, Mr. Camdzic, a criminal investigation was launched into the circumstances of his death? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never given any instructions to initiate an investigation of that kind. I personally never received any such instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. President, if the witness could be shown P135. I may have prepared some copies for Your Honours, and this might refresh your recollection -- or perhaps you have another comment to make. Mr. President, that's a one-page document dated forwards 29th January 1993 from the assistant commander for security, Nesib Talic, of the 7th Muslim Brigade, and it addresses the murderer of "our company commander, Elvedin Camdzic, who was immediately arrested" -- and it talks about an alleged perpetrator who was "immediately arrested and taken to the district military prison."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just take your time to read it. Do you remember that a gentleman called Cvijanovic was arrested and taken to the military -- district military prison in connection with the killing of a company commander from the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally do not remember Mr. Cvijanovic, and if this is so, then it is in accordance with the rules when there is reason to believe that there was a crime committed. Mr. Nesib Talic is addressing himself to the security organ of the 3rd Corps, and again this is in accordance with the norms of reporting and requests for information. I don't remember that the chief of the security sector gave me personally any concrete tasks linked to this information or linked to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know whether the killing of Mr. Camdzic might have been a battle casualty? Have you any information about that?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have occasion to see combat reports, nor can I say that this was treated in that way, but it is quite certain that the killing of any member, and especially a company commander, is a loss for the forces, and it is probably contained in the combat reports from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And following that, because it's a loss for the forces, it needs to be fully investigated; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes, but it's not to say that there's always an investigation when there is a loss of this kind. Since this specific information was forwarded to a concrete organ of control and command, then the security sector -- or rather, the chief of that sector on the basis of that report initiates investigative work in order to collect evidence and potentially submit reports to the competent court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me leave Dusina and go on to a different location, but we are staying in -- in those days, 27th January 1993. Do you remember that on that day the military battalion had received an order from the commander of the 3rd Corps to -- for a military police patrol to patrol a unit which came from the 7th Mountain Muslim Brigade, from Zenica to Turbe and back? Do you remember having received an order from the 3rd Corps commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to ask my learned friend to clarify. It's either a problem with the translation or I can't understand what it says here. He said "on that same day," "in those days." I don't know what he meant, whether he's talking about the day of fighting in Dusina on the 26th of January, because I see here the date is the 27th of January, and the question was "on that same day," or, rather, "in those days." So I'm not sure what day he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I probably misspoke. It's on the -- this incident occurred, I believe, on the 27th of -- of January. And it's not related to Dusina, I believe. So -- and of course we all know Dusina occurred on the 26th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: On the 27th of January, do you remember having received an order from the commander of the 3rd Corps for a military police patrol to bring units pertaining to the 7th Mountain -- Muslim Mountain Brigade from Zenica to Turbe and back? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I do remember. The order was very brief, I think, but it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. resulted from the obligations of the military police. The Military Police Battalion had the obligation or duty in certain situations on the basis of the corps commander's assessment to provide traffic or secure the movement of columns of military vehicles, columns of ABiH members, et cetera. That's one thing. And secondly, since the tensions were high, that the conflict had already started, and members of the HVO had a very negative attitude towards members of the 7th Brigade, the commander decided to engage the military battalion to secure the column, the main aim being to reduce tensions and eliminate the possibility of any incident breaking out along the route from Zenica to Turbe and back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember whether that location in the Turbe area was in fact Bijelo Bucje? That's where your patrol was supposed to bring the units to and back?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether it was Bijelo Bucje. I know the order said "Zenica-Turbe, Turbe-Zenica." For me, the final destination was Turbe, and I really don't remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The first entry in the 3rd Corps logbook which mentions Bijelo Bucje. I just wanted to -- to inquire whether that's a possibility as well, if you know, if you don't know.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would just like to -- to follow up on the comment you made about the very negative attitude towards the members of the 7th Brigade by the HVO. Why do you say that? Can you give us an explanation?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you watched one -- saw one of the Defence exhibits, in 1992 the Military Police Battalion already had some problems when it came to engaging Croats. All units of the BH army were characterised by the Croat extremists, especially the extremists in the HVO, as Mujahedin units, as Muslim and I don't know what else. If a Military Police Battalion encountered such problems, then you can imagine what it was like to be a member of a unit which had in its name the word "Muslim" and in which a large number of members, because of their religious beliefs, are wearing beards, and the extremists in the HVO see them as a threat to their own interests and probably all this contributed to the heightening of tensions to such an extent that this became a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you talked about the number of individuals that were detained by your services in -- in quite a number of documents: For instance - and I don't think we need to go into that again - tab 39. That's the August 1993 report, for the month of August. And it talks about 256 individuals. Now, in your time as the commander of the -- the military police, was there ever -- were there ever foreigners, including so-called Mujahedin, who were detained in your facilities?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the Military Police Battalion having detained anyone who called himself a Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, were certain forms used by your service, pre-printed forms which had blanks left in for the individual details of people who were supposed to be taken in for custody?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such forms did exist in accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure, and they would be filled in with the particulars of the person who may be taken into custody on various grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would it refresh your memory if I would show you such a form in which the name of such a Mujahedin was mentioned? Would that refresh your memory as to whether such a person would -- was indeed arrested by your service?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps my learned friend could be more specific as to the time he's asking the witness about; that is, whether in their custody there were any foreigners, because it says here "while you were performing your duties." Perhaps the time covered by the indictment would be best. Are we talking about 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's exactly my question. I asked him, you know -- and that must have been stuck out in his memory, whether there was ever something. He said "no." And it doesn't matter which time period it is. It will refresh his memory. We'll see what -- what date does -- I can certainly state the date. It's January 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember that in January 1994 somebody was taken custody by -- by your services?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that, and I think the misunderstanding had to do with the dates, because from 1994 onwards we did have situations in which the so-called Mujahedin we had to investigate into and take into custody in accordance with the law. In 1994 -- or rather, at the end of 1993, a similar activity was launched in connection with the Golub operation, which the security sector coordinated and its counter-intelligence body, the aim being to establish the facts with respect to, conditionally speaking, a military unit that called itself "legal" and which existed in the area of Zenica. We knew it under the name of the so-called Turkish Guerilla. And the coordination of all these activities was done by the security sector and its counter-intelligence sector. In addition to operatives from the Military Police Battalion, some operatives from the CSB were engaged, and important for this operation was that these members were not members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina or of the 3rd Corps, and it was not possible to engage anyone from the brigade, such as the assistant commander for security, as was the case for Operation Golub. So these persons were monitored, with the aim of establishing their organisational structure, their movements, et cetera, and I remember that following instructions from the sector, together with the CSB we did arrest a group of men. We processed them. They were held for 72 hours, as provided for by the Law on Procedure, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Why did you arrest these people despite the fact that, as you state, they were not members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for that very reason, because they weren't ABiH members and they had declared themselves as members. They were often in uniform. They were seen in various situations. And I believe that they even committed certain crimes. They would sell cigarettes on the black market, et cetera. And the security sector had this information. They gathered all the information and we were the executive organ, in terms of carrying out what the security sector had accomplished in the operative sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in fact, your services, your battalion, talked to a number of these what you called Turkish Guerillas, took witness statements from them.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. As I said, apart from the operative aspect, we were also the executive organ for the security sector. They had a small number of operative officers and they carried out certain duties, such as counter-intelligence, et cetera. When it comes to going into the field, arresting individuals, processing them, taking statements, gathering evidence, this is usually something that the Military Police Battalion does. I think that you'll find similarities between this Turkish Guerilla group and the Green League. The system of gathering information was the same. And the military police carries out the plan at the site itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you recall that when your services interviewed these members of the Turkish Guerilla, that some of them stated that they were members of the Army of the ABiH? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'll go back to the chain of command: Firstly, there wasn't a single case while I was in command in which I directly participated in taking statements from any individuals, so I never interpreted the contents of statements. I left that to the commander of the platoon for military police investigations. After he had carried out his activities, he'd provide summary information on certain important elements. I am not familiar with there being anything of that nature contained in the statements taken from those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would it help you if I would show you one of these statements taken by one of your subordinates? I take it -- in fact, it's Mr. Alispahic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that my learned colleague is going beyond the scope of your decision. He asked the witness whether he was familiar with the event. He asked him whether he knew how the battalion participated in the event. The witness quite clearly stated that he couldn't remember that, that he never took any statements. And now we're moving on to questions about the contents of statements. And this is beyond the scope allowed for cross-examination in accordance with the decision that you rendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could just add to what Mrs. Residovic said, and that is that, as my learned friend indicated, Mr. Alispahic did participate in taking the statement, but so did Mr. Semir Saric, who was a witness who testified, as Your Honours will know, this week Monday, and his name appears on this statement, and yet this statement was not shown to -- to that witness. In our submission, as my learned colleague said yesterday, that would have been the right person to put the statement to because he was the one involved in it. This witness has said that he was not involved in these statements or analysing these statements, and he's not familiar with anything that was in these statements. It's not going to assist him in refreshing his memory if he's now shown a statement. But in addition to that, Your Honour, the real issue here is that my learned friend is putting an assertion about the fact that certain foreigners were in the army, and he's asking the witness whether he knows that from these statements. If he wants to put that assertion, he can. The witness can -- can then answer it. But what some other witness said in a statement cannot be evidence, and if he's trying to get that as evidence, then -- then we do object to that. If he wants to make the assertion that foreigners were in the army, he can say that to the witness and let's see what the witness's answer is. If he wants to call a witness who -- who might have said in a statement, well, then that's a separate matter. That witness should have been called. But he can't try and use what another person has said and bring that into evidence through this witness. That was the main objection that I was making at the beginning. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I might respond first to what my learned colleague from the Hadzihasanovic said. It's well within the scope, I believe, of cross-examination. The witness himself volunteered the term of "Turkish Guerilla" and he displayed quite some knowledge. And indeed he has to; he was the command to have military police. That was his job to know what was happening in that area. And again, in -- in response to what Mr. Dixon has said, that's not evidence when I put something to the witness. It's up to the witness to tell from his knowledge, from his experience what he knows about that. But -- and we are free to put anything to whatever witness comes. It's up to me or to my colleagues to decide which documents to use with which witness. Mr. Alispahic, I don't think he appeared as a witness, so that's the first time we have the military commander and one of his subordinates, direct subordinates - Alispahic was one of the commanders below him - has taken a statement, and the purpose of it is merely to show him the statement and ask him does he know something about that. He might say, "No, that's new to me," "yes, I remember it now," or "no, the statement is totally unreliable because my interviewers put words into the mouth of the witness." That's what he can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I don't want to keep this going unnecessarily, but it is important to note that Mr. Saric's name is on the document as well as Mr. Alispahic, so both of them were involved in taking the statement. Mr. Saric has certainly testified here. He did so on Monday as a subordinate of the -- the current witness before Your Honours. And I'm looking at the original. He has signed this document as well. In addition to that, Mr. Alispahic was somebody the Prosecution interviewed. They took a statement from him. And that statement was disclosed to us under Rule 68. He wasn't called as a witness by the Prosecution. A statement was taken. And once again, another opportunity was lost, in our submission, by the Prosecution if they wanted to introduce this as evidence. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, several points: Again, and I can only repeat it, I don't want to use it as evidence. Evidence is only what the witness is going to say: Yes, no, I remember, I recall. And a second point - I'm repeating it - I can use any information I want with this witness. If I -- it's not the best-evidence rule here that we have to get the best witness for the best document and only for that purpose. I can show something which is reasonably within the scope of this gentleman. He's the commander, Mr. President, of the Military Police Battalion. A direct subordinate of him took a witness statement, and I can certainly ask him after he has said that these statements are usually reliable what this means, what it's all about. He can say no, Mr. President, if he doesn't recall it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're wasting time. The debate arises because the questions that should have been put to the witness weren't put to him. One should have asked the witness, who spontaneously mentioned the investigations into the Turkish Guerilla -- one should have asked the witness who conducted the investigation. The answer: Alispahic. And then he should have been asked who forwarded the results of the investigation to the judge or to the prosecutor. The witness could have replied, "It was me" or, "It was Alispahic." If he said that he did that, then he should have been asked whether he had read the statements taken in the course of the investigation. One should have proceeded by putting such questions to the witness and this would have enabled us to avoid a discussion that is of no use. We have four minutes, so please start from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, do you know who was in charge? Was there a specific who was in charge of these investigations against the Turkish Guerilla?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire investigation, operative information, preparations to arrest individuals, et cetera, was conducted by the Sector for Military Security in the 3rd Corps, and I think that the chief of the counter-intelligence organ, Mr. Osman Vlajcic, was responsible to coordinate and lead all aspects of the investigation. On the basis of everything that has been said so far, the Military Police Battalion had the duty after arrests were made and statements were taken to provide their files to the military security service and together with the statements and information that they had, they would assess what further measures should be taken in accordance with the law and they would then instruct the Military Police Battalion and provide them with guidelines as to how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So who within your services would forward these witness statements to the security service, military security service?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Military Police Battalion had the duty to complete all the statements and then via the battalion command he had to forward them to the security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When you compiled several witness statements and did forward it to your subordinate officer did you attach a cover letter, or how was that done, practically?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The accompanying letter meant that statements would be attached to the document, nothing else. My comments and comments from my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. subordinates weren't necessary because there was a service that coordinated all those activities. It was on the basis of those statements - and I'll repeat this - that we would receive instructions or an oral order or other orders on taking further measures and on completing -- or rather, finalising investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So it was you who did send this package of witness statements to your superior office.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the commander of the battalion, myself, my deputy also had authority to sign a document in which one explained that statements had been attached to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When sending these documents to the superior command, were you, as the commander of the Military Police Battalion, generally aware of what's contained in a file which you passed on to your superior command?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, I didn't read these statements or any others, nor did I comment on them. Comments were based on the report from the command of the military police platoon for investigations, and that was quite sufficient for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you were familiar with the investigation against the Turkish Guerilla.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was familiar with it to the extent that the security sector believed that they should inform me of it. My knowledge concerned the engagement of authorised officials when taking statements -- or rather, it concerned the members of the Military Police Battalion who had brought in individuals and interviewed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, were you informed by your superiors that indeed members who declared themselves --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll stop now because we have to have our technical break. How much time does the Prosecution need to complete its cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Including legal arguments, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If there are no major legal arguments, I would say 10 minutes should be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And how much time will you require for re-examination? I'm asking you this question because the registrar has answered my question. If we have a hearing tomorrow, we can only commence at 4.00 p.m. because we're too late for the morning session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecution has raised a number of issues, and I'd like to ask the witness about these issues again, so I believe that we will need -- or I will need at least another half an hour to examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ten minutes, plus one hour, well, that's perhaps possible. We'll see. But try to be concise and perhaps we can proceed expeditiously. Very well. We'll resume at five to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask both parties to be as concise as possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think, after having laid the foundation, it is established that formally the documents, the witness statements, went over the desk of -- of the commander of the military police. He also showed general knowledge about what was going on because he was informed by his subordinates and by his superiors. He volunteered that there was an investigation about the -- the Turkish Guerilla. And he also, as the military police commander, he's responsible for what was happening in his area. And he testified he assigned the interviewers to these interviews. So I think I'm entitled just for the specific purpose of showing him whether he was aware that from the witness statements information came out that members of the Turkish Guerilla were part, in their own words, of the 7th Muslim Brigade. Again, it's up to him to say, "I've heard of it. I" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But there's something missing. When the case was -- when the file was forwarded, did he see the file? Did he sign it? That's what's missing. Because if it's his subordinate who dealt with the file behind his back, or rather, without his knowledge, then he might not be familiar with it. So there's a question that's missing, to know whether this file was forwarded to him. Did he see it? Did he sign it? Was it his deputy who signed it? So there are two or three questions that still need to be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were there instances that witness statements, indeed files, left your command and went to your superior command without your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall whether any files being produced in the course the investigation into the Turkish Guerilla left your office without your -- your knowledge, your general knowledge? Have you heard about -- are you aware of any instances like that?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say that I remember any such cases, but in practice it was possible that the security -- the military security sector might establish direct contact with the Military Police Platoon for Investigations in order to carry out tasks more expeditiously, tasks for the purpose of investigations. And secondly, if there were no such documents -- or if there was no contact between the security sector and the military investigations platoon, then someone I had left up there - my deputy or some other authorised official - might forward those documents without me being familiar with all the elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But in relation to a specific investigation like this one about the Turkish Guerilla, you can't say whether it's you who have personally forwarded these files to your superior command? You can't say with certainty, but you wouldn't exclude it.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every investigation is specific. I can't claim anything for sure, but I can claim for sure that the battalion's mission was accomplished because statements were taken and forwarded to the security sector. As to whether I'd see them or not, as to whether I'd sign an accompanying document or not, in this case and in any other case this wasn't an important question. It was important for the authorised official from the Military Police Battalion and authorised officials to carry out the tasks that had been assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I were to show you a document, a two- or three-page witness statement, do you think it might refresh your recollection of whether you have seen it before forwarding it to your superior command? Is there a chance that would enlighten your knowledge about whether it passed your desk or not?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement itself won't help to refresh my memory. I'd said that as a rule I did not read statements, because this was done at a lower level of the chain of command. This would have meant that I didn't believe the subordinate commander of military police investigations. All I could do is perhaps confirm the reliability of the statement. But again, I'll repeat that this would not really refresh my memory. It wouldn't help me to tell you whether it was on my desk or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But your subordinate commanders would usually inform you about what's contained in general in these statements; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it concerned something that they believed they should inform me about. But believe me, the commander receives so much information every day that I couldn't say that I would focus on certain aspects of a investigation on a certain day, on a certain week. My subordinates informed me about the tasks they carried out, on -- about the duties they had to perform in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's as far as I can take it. It may be enough. It may be not. I'm absolutely in your hands whether I can show it to the witness to refresh his memory. Credibility might be a different aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll withdraw now. --- Break taken at 1.03 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber will now render its third oral decision today. Perhaps it's not the last one. Given that the witness has told the Chamber in response to a Prosecution question that he didn't sign files that were forwarded and he didn't read statements taken from witnesses, the Trial Chamber believes that it's not necessary to show the witness this document. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, were you aware that one of your subordinate interviewers, Mr. Alispahic, interviewed a person who told him that he was a member of the RBiH army since April 1993 as a Guerilla and this person had a dual nationality in -- from Turkey and from Bosnia? Were you aware of -- of a situation like -- like that, that somebody who appears to be Turkish Guerilla in fact told one of your investigators that he was a member of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't understood the question. You said that one of my members was an investigator and a member of the ABiH -- could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. It may have been a little bit too quick. One of your subordinates, Mr. Alispahic, interviewed a person and this person - in fact, I can name him - Mehmed Turcin, he asked dual citizenship from Turkey and from Bosnia, and he told your investigator, Mr. Alispahic, that he was a member of the ABiH army since April 1993 and part of the Guerilla. Do you think that's -- that's correct, when Mr. Alispahic noted that down?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know whether that's correct or not. What I do know is that when individuals give statements, and in particular to authorised officials from the Military Police Battalion, and when an investigation is launched into them, and when they might be charged for certain crimes, they then use all the methods they can avail themselves of in order to find evidence, false statements, et cetera, which might prevent them from being prosecuted. So I'm really not familiar with this case. I'm not familiar with this gentleman having stated that he was a member of the army at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you have heard of instances that people called "Guerilla" were considering themselves vis-a-vis your investigators as members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Have you heard of instances?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they were brought in in 1994, I believe that at the time they were already members of the army, and that's what I was interested in then. But in legal terms, as to whether they were members of the army during the period that you have mentioned, well, I'm quite sure that the military security sector would have had such information and wouldn't have prepared operative activities in order to arrest them and hand them over to the authorities. This would have been done directly through the units that they were members of, through the security organ, through military police units, in units that they were members of, in invented commas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: To pick up a point before we left before the break. I was about to show you one of these pre-printed forms which are the decision in relation to an arrest of a person. Who is normally filling in that information? The title is "In accordance to Article 196 of the Law on Criminal Procedure, the authorised official of the Battalion Military Police reached the following decision ..." And then it's a printed text and then it's filled in, who is to be taken into custody. Who is usually filling in that information by hand?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually this information is filled in by an authorised official from the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I'm not sure whether you had answered before the break my question: You agree with me that in -- in January 1994, in fact, people who were declared on that form as a member of the Mujahedin were indeed put into custody, into your detention facilities. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't confirm the first and last names, but I know that a group from the so-called Guerilla, according to the information I already mentioned -- I know that they were interviewed and that pursuant to instructions from the Sector for Intelligence a number of the Guerilla members were taken into custody in accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure and in order to prepare criminal reports to be filed against them with the prosecutor's office. I really can't remember their first and last names, nor was this of particular interest to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. President, this is the document I mentioned which had been acquired by the OTP after the end of the Prosecution case and I would propose this exhibit, after having it shown to the witness, perhaps he can confirm that comes out of the military police, to have it admitted later as a full exhibit -- exhibit with full value, if that's amenable, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a -- it's a form. It's a standard document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, filled in and stamped by one of the members of the military police. It's not stamped. I can put it onto the ELMO, Mr. President, if -- if ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You can show this document, but it's not a piece of evidence. It's just so that the witness can say that this document was used within the military police. Please place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's number 19 of my bundle. I believe I have an exhibit -- an English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just clarify one matter. I know the document is going to be shown to the witness. By my learned friend seemed to indicate that it can be introduced as an exhibit. Our understanding of Your Honours' decision is that all new documents, it doesn't mart when they were obtained, if they were not use in the Prosecution case, then they can't be used as exhibits now. The Prosecution may, of course, reapply to reopen their case at a later stage, but our position is that all documents fit into the same category. If they were not in the Prosecution case, then they are new documents which could only be introduced for a limited purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with my learned colleague. I just would like to show it, if he can tell us the authenticity of the document. Perhaps we can later use it at a later stage in the proceedings. If it could be put onto the ELMO. Perhaps, maybe -- I mean, we can -- we can hand over the whole bundle now - it may take some time - to the Defence if they want it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The only point of showing this document to the witness would be for the witness to say that it's a standard document used by the military police. That's all. Unless perhaps this document never existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we first see this and see whether there's any information contained in the document. If it does contain information, you have already decided that it can't be shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Prosecution, is this document being shown to the witness in its form? It's not the contents of the document that the witness is being asked to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, it appears that it's a form and a member of his police form has filled in the details of a Mujahedin who is to -- supposed to be taken into custody. But I think the Defence has not seen Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But if you're saying that this document refers to a Mujahedin, which means you are going to introduce the question of the Mujahedin. We only want to know whether this document was used in the case of detention of persons, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We don't need to go any further. I withdraw the document. Just a few remaining questions, if I may, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember that in -- in June 1993 - in fact, on 17th of June - you submitted a short report to the -- to your superior authorities, I believe, that the security situation in Zenica wasn't -- wasn't proper, wasn't perfect? I think you -- you mentioned that improper conduct of armed soldiers, that they take cigarettes and alcohol away, stop girls wearing miniskirts, and so on. Do you remember having put that on record and -- and sent up to your -- your command, comments like that about the situation in the town of -- of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say that I remember the document, but it is quite certain that in the description of tasks of the Military Police Battalion it is provided for that we should inform our superior about such developments, and that is the chief of the security sector. So it is quite probable that I did write a report of that kind and forwarded it to my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you remember having said you had received oral admonitions from some people that your military police be polite and careful when approaching members of the 7th Muslim Brigade? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was happening at the time was that for the first time we see soldiers that we had not been accustomed to seeing in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the last 40 to 50 years. The Rules of Service that was in force at the time envisaged, among other things, that a soldier should look like a soldier, buttoned up, with a belt, clean-shaven, and everything else. My suggestions with respect to the 7th Muslim Brigade was that the Military Police Battalion through its admonishments of members of the 7th Brigade should bear in mind that in that brigade there were soldiers who for religious reasons are wearing a beard, which means they differ from the standard appearance of a soldier. So my suggestions were along those lines. And also, the question of beards could be addressed, and this appeared not only in the 7th but also in the 314th Brigade, especially in Zenica. I think there were some also in the 303rd Brigade. But no other instructions did I give about any cases of drastic violations of the rules did we receive as the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That concludes cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now the Defence. Go to the substance, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please show the witness P328, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mujezinovic, my learned friend asked you several questions about the competencies of the military police and the battalion of military police, and I would just like before passing on to any other questions, I would like to remind you of what you said, that your purview and tasks were defined by the Rules of Service. Is that the Rules of Service that you have in front of you that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at paragraph 1 on page 3, which is entitled "Purview of the military police." And in that point 1, towards the bottom, it says: "To discover and intercept criminal activities involving members of the armed forces or other citizens but only in cases when the object of criminal offence is military property or criminal offences within the jurisdiction of military courts." Is this a binding rule that you were guided by, and all other military units?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All military police units, including the battalion, were guided by this rule in their activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: When other citizens are involved, who was meant? Was it just civilians, citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina? But did this also apply to foreign citizens who were not members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Did this apply to all other citizens regardless of their nationality or citizenship?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it refers to all citizens, regardless of citizenship or ethnicity. The main aim was being to take measures envisaged by the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell me once again: When those persons did not commit offences at the expense of the armed forces or acts within the jurisdiction of the military courts, which is the only authorised police authority that could act in relation to them?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only authorised authority was the civilian police -- or rather, members of the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When the corps commander issued orders, who did those orders refer to? The army, these other persons, or were they general so that anyone could implement them?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Corps commander's orders are exclusively linked to the military organisation. The corps commander commands units within the 3rd Corps, and he is the only one authorised to issue orders, guidelines, and instructions to units' members of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to one of the questions of my learned friend, you said that you trust your subordinates when they file reports, that you have no reason to doubt the correctness and truthfulness of those reports; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it a general rule in the army that the superior officer should have confidence in the information and reports received and the execution of tasks by subordinate officers or units?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, that is the general rule. And that is why there is a chain of command. So everyone is accountable at his level and also at the levels defined by mutual relationships.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, will you look at document at tab 51, please. It is DH161/4. The document has been addressed by the commander of the 3rd Corps to the Military Police Battalion, and in item 3 it says that "For the execution of this task, the commander of the Military Police Battalion is held accountable." Were you the responsible person for executing this task and which should report back about the execution of that task to the corps command?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to this order, I was to resubordinate two units to the 325th Brigade, so I had to prepare this and to send the unit to the required place, and I am, of course, duty-bound to report to the corps commander about the completion of the task.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know why such an order was being issued? In the preamble, it says: "To assist in preventing undisciplined behaviour and looting." Who was -- who needed disciplining according to this order?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably members of units within the 3rd Corps who were deployed in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at now document at tab 42. It is a document dated the 10th of June, 1993 of the command of the 3rd Corps, DH161/12. In paragraph 6, it says that "Brigade commanders will be held responsible and other commanding officers." Can we see from this order who needs to implement the order and who the commander has to trust that he will indeed carry out the order as ordered?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander needs to trust his subordinate brigade commanders and other subordinate commanding officers. By appointing brigade commanders or commanders of units at lower levels, this means that they enjoy the confidence of their superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at paragraph 2 in the preamble where it says: "A conflict between the HVO and the army would sometimes develop into open armed conflicts and combat activities lead to highly harmful behaviour with unforeseeable consequences." Does this preamble, too, confirm which is envisaged by the rules, and that is that the commander issues an order simply to discipline his own members, or can his order apply also to measures to be taken against other persons?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander's order implies taking measures exclusively in relation to members of the ABiH or, rather, members of the 3rd Corps because probably these matters are not within the jurisdiction of military courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at document at tab 47, which my learned friend showed to you. It is DH161/13. And in the preamble of this order, it says: "Soldiers obsessed with war booty, stolen things, forget the tasks they were given, reject your orders by which they are endangering their own destiny." Tell me, please: In view of the cause that has prompted this order, does this order apply to persons over which the military police has jurisdiction, or can it apply to some other persons as well?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, the order applies to fighters, members of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH, as is clear from the preamble. The rest is defined by the law and the Rules of Service and the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: My learned friend asked you several questions about the Mujahedin Guerilla, and you spoke about counter-intelligence and other activities that preceded this military police operation. Tell me, for how long, to the best of your recollection, did the counter-intelligence section of the armed forces engage in prior investigations in order to launch their operation?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This took about five or six months of intensive monitoring, operative work on the ground, and collecting evidence as part of the investigations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend also asked you whether you were ever assigned to investigate war crimes. You answered that you investigated events without bothering about the classification of acts. At what stage is a certain act legally qualified? Do you first name an act and then investigate it, or the other way round?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The process of qualifying a criminal offence runs as follows: By going on site, the military police engages in pre-trial activities to establish what kind of criminal act may have been committed. They collect sufficient material evidence, and then on the basis of that evidence, they may propose the qualification of the act. The prosecutor may accept or reject the criminal report and proposes to the investigative judge the legal qualification of the act. So it is the judge who finally decides what kind of criminal offence had been committed. So the military police only makes a proposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you investigated the event which you suspected could be a criminal offence, did the corps commander or your chief of security ever prohibit you from investigating an event which might have elements of a crime?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just any such event, but no other event was I ever told by my superiors not to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend asked you whether it was normal to conduct an investigation when a commander gets killed. Tell me, as you were in the war for four years, is it normal for people to get killed in battle?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's normal, especially by commanders, who have to set the example by their bravery.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, that thousands of men were killed, was it customary to conduct an investigation for each of the dead persons, why, and how he was killed?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not customary at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this Turkish Guerilla, you said you didn't know what they said later on because when someone is a suspect, he seeks to belittle his responsibility. To the best of your knowledge, in 1993 was this Turkish Guerilla within the 3rd Corps or any of its units?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not have occasion to see a single document or to establish in any other way that they were members. And the counter-intelligence work in the security sector and preparations for arrest did not discover that. Had they been members, no such evidence was ever found.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you look at document at tab 80, also shown to you by my learned friend. In view of the fact that in answer to my question you explained when you were responsible for civilians, here in (B), it says that "The criminal reports were filed for 204 [Realtime transcript read in error "804"] civilians." Were they civilians in your jurisdiction, according to the decree on military courts, or could these be any other civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were civilians for which we were responsible -- or rather, the acts emanating from the Law on District Military Courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please look at document, at 79, the plan of action Golub. You have already said that that operation, too, was prepared for five or six months, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From this plan -- or rather, before I ask you anything about the plan itself. For you as a military policeman, is it normal before launching a military police operation, arrest, or investigation, is it important for you to discover all the basic elements required to be able to plan and prepare the number of policemen you need for the execution of that task and the consequences that may result?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The more information we had or any occasion we had to avoid casualties or other elements, we had to collect. So it's quite normal and binding by law to collect all relevant information when it comes to perpetrators of crimes, that is, how well equipped they are, how skilled, what methods they resort to, nicknames, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you, as the battalion commander, engage in a military police operation without knowing at all what you would come across?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, because that would mean exposing my men to absolute risk.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at this plan. In addition to the fact indicated by my colleague on page 2 that you knew that this group had pistols, automatic weapons, hand grenades, et cetera, you also knew how many people there were. On page 1, there were 12. Is it important for you to know the number of men?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it is important, because we had to send a patrol to arrest each of these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that you are aware of their addresses and even the floor on which they live. Tell me, is it important for you to know where the persons you wish to arrest are located?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The address, the entrance, the floor is very important. Also, whether there's any possibility of leaving those apartments across balconies or escaping through any openings, because once you arrive on site, it's not sufficient to appear at the door, but you always have to block the whole area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it important to know whether these ten persons may be supported by another ten, who might resist you?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The potential danger existed that they might arouse the rest of their supporters and the rest of the unit and we could have an armed rebellion within our forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I see that you planned 95 policemen for these persons, 90 automatic rifles, and some other ammunition and weaponry. If this -- did you use significant human and materiel resources for these 12 men?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The high degree of criminality and -- of this group we needed to mobilise a large number of men and resources so as not to be put in a position of failing due to inappropriate planning and preparations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a commander, if you were in a position with respect to this group or the Turkish Guerilla or any other group, if you had to deal with such problems in various ways, where would you rank resort to military force if you had other possibilities to deal with the problem as well?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The use of military force as a means to be used by the military police comes at the end, which means once you have exhausted all possibilities and when you see that there's no other way, only then does the police resort to the use of force.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With respect to this arrest, regardless of the fact that you mobilised a large number of men to do it, at that point in time did this reduce the capability of your battalion to engage in other duties at the same time, or were the elements you had collected sufficient for you to carry out this operation without any negative consequences for the battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operation was planned for a long time. Everything was done to keep the preparations secret and confidential, so that we used our reserves, so that our other activities would not suffer. Just to carry out the arrest and neglect our other duties would not be proper nor lawful.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To go back to the Guerilla, in view of the fact that there were foreigners there: Do you know, as the battalion commander, on the basis of counter-intelligence information whether the 3rd Corps had to have the approval of a superior command before launching an operation against foreigners?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, I was not involved in that area, but I know that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, your testimony has been completed. Thank you for coming to testify, and on behalf of the Chamber, I wish you all the best for your return home. And could the usher please accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the very little time left, you are going to tell us about your plans next week, because we don't have the time to do it now. If my understanding is correct, next Monday we will begin with the expert witness; Tuesday we will have Witness X interposed; and perhaps towards the end of the testimony of X we will continue with the expert witness Wednesday and Thursday; then there's a holiday; and we will resume on Tuesday. Is that right? Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in order to avoid any misunderstanding, I know that yesterday my colleague made some comments regarding the examination-in-chief of the expert. I wish to say that the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic will take 12 hours for the examination-in-chief. When the Prosecution presented their report, they had a different strategy; however, we have sufficient material to have three complete sittings with this witness. We can either follow with the cross-examination that same week, or we can have him come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So 12 hours, that means three days for you. Let's hope there will be no repetition during those 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I promise you that, Mr. President. We have many subjects to address with the expert, and I promise you that you will not be disappointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we await that with impatience. If the Prosecution has no special points to address and raise, I invite everyone to come back for the hearing that will begin on Monday at 2.15. As there are no witnesses for tomorrow and the day after, we will resume our work on Monday at 2.15, and on that day at the beginning we will address the question of admission of documents. I will give you the floor. And then you will see whether you need to talk about the schedule, and then we will begin with the testimony of the expert witness. Thank you all. And I invite you to come back on Monday at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 21st day of March, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
